title: Kubernetes
description: 27 lessons progress from reconciliation and ready Services to scoped security, storage, jobs, scaling, templating, GitOps and recovery, with offline checks and a guarded dedicated local lab.
level: Foundations → intermediate practice with optional systems labs
prerequisites: Complete Delivery & Operations (delivery-operations) containers/build/runtime exercises first; React (react), .NET (dotnet) and SQL Server (sql-server) retain their own application/data responsibilities.
Python 3.14+ for offline checks. A dedicated local kind cluster is opt-in and requires compatible Docker/Linux containers, kind and kubectl; no cloud account required.
outcomes: Trace declarative objects through controllers, scheduling, kubelet and ready endpoints.
Read consistent labels/selectors/ports and understand ConfigMap/Secret lifecycle boundaries.
Design distinct probes, requests/limits and compatible rollout/placement decisions.
Review non-root Pod security, scoped RBAC and enforced network-policy evidence.
Explain PVC/Job/HPA/PDB guarantees and prerequisites with bounded local exercises.
Render Helm, reason about GitOps drift and separate cluster/application recovery stores.
setup: Run python -m unittest -v test_release_app.py check_manifests.py from the extracted flat kit.
JSON manifests use stable Kubernetes API versions; offline contract checks do not prove full schema admission or live behavior.
For an opted-in dedicated kind cluster, follow README.md exactly: verify context/loopback endpoint, build/load image, Bootstrap namespace, Validate server dry-run, then Apply.
Read optional-manifest prerequisites before network policy, storage, HPA or identity tests; no add-ons/cloud/cluster mutations occur merely by reading the course.
nextSteps: Implement an external durable data owner and real authenticated application before using replicated service state.
Study CNI/CSI behavior, secure cluster lifecycle and controller design with measured failure-domain evidence.
Keep Helm/GitOps controllers and privileges separately reviewed; rendered YAML is not a live guarantee.
Plan and execute protected provider-specific backup/recovery and upgrade drills before production use.

lessons.title: 1. Identify the problem Kubernetes solves
lessons.takeaway: Kubernetes coordinates container workloads through declarative API objects and controllers.

sections.title: Workloads and controllers
paragraphs: Kubernetes uses API objects and controllers to schedule containers, replace failed Pods and route service traffic. Applications still need correct transactions and backups. Start with the working container from Delivery & Operations, then distinguish application failures from scheduler or control-plane failures. The supplied image runs the Python/SQLite lab. It does not run the React/.NET/SQL stack.

sections.title: Replicas with scratch data
paragraphs: Every local replica has its own scratch SQLite file. Use /version and health endpoints for replicated exercises; notes are not a shared durable service. A real stateful API needs an external data owner or a carefully designed single-writer storage pattern.
sections.example:
Desired: 2 stateless web replicas
Observed: 1 replica running
Controller attempts replacement; scheduler chooses a node; kubelet starts containers.

exercise.prompt: List which responsibilities remain with the application.
exercise.solution: Authentication, authorization, transaction/idempotency rules, compatible schemas and recoverable data remain application/service responsibilities. Kubernetes can restart a broken process but cannot infer the correct business outcome.
checks: Distinguish platform and application invariants.
Identify replicated scratch-data limits.

quiz.question: Which application property must be designed separately from Deployment replica reconciliation?
options: A controller attempting to reconcile the desired Pod count.
Shared, correct note storage across replicas.
Separate Pod identities for the requested replicas.
quiz.explanation: Shared, correct note storage across replicas. Authentication, authorization, transaction/idempotency rules, compatible schemas and recoverable data remain application/service responsibilities. Kubernetes can restart a broken process but cannot infer the correct business outcome.

lessons.title: 2. Trace API server, etcd, scheduler and kubelet
lessons.takeaway: The API server exposes the cluster API, etcd stores cluster state, controllers reconcile objects and the scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to nodes.

sections.title: Control-plane responsibilities
paragraphs: The API server exposes the cluster API, etcd stores cluster state, controllers reconcile objects and the scheduler assigns unscheduled Pods to nodes. Kubelets act on assigned Pod specifications through container runtimes. These roles explain why accepting a Deployment does not mean a container is already healthy. Desired state and observed status are different parts of the object contract.

sections.title: Pending versus failed startup
paragraphs: If the scheduler cannot find capacity, a Pod can remain Pending even though the API request succeeded. If an image is missing, the node may be assigned but container startup fails. Inspect the actual status/events before changing unrelated YAML.
sections.example:
kubectl apply → API stores desired Deployment
Deployment controller → ReplicaSet → Pods
scheduler → node assignment
kubelet → pull/start → probes/status

exercise.prompt: Place an unsatisfied resource request and an image-pull error on the trace.
exercise.solution: Insufficient resources prevent assignment at scheduling; an unavailable image fails after node assignment during kubelet/runtime startup. Both differ from an API validation rejection before the object is accepted.
checks: Name the responsible component.
Separate admission, scheduling and startup.

quiz.question: Which component assigns an unscheduled Pod to a node?
quiz.explanation: The scheduler selects a node for an unscheduled Pod subject to placement and resource constraints. The kubelet and container runtime handle startup on the assigned node.

lessons.title: 3. Create an opt-in local lab with context guards
lessons.takeaway: kubectl uses a kubeconfig context to choose cluster and identity, so a valid command can affect the wrong environment.

sections.title: Cluster context and identity
paragraphs: `kubectl` uses a kubeconfig context to choose cluster and identity, so a valid command can affect the wrong environment. The lab names its kind cluster `notebook-lab`, producing `kind-notebook-lab`, and every mutating example names that context and `notebook-lab` namespace. `lab.ps1` refuses another context or a non-loopback API endpoint before making a cluster request.

sections.title: Local tool and endpoint checks
paragraphs: These commands consume local machine resources and are optional; no cloud account or provider provisioning is needed. Install compatible current kubectl/kind/Docker tools yourself, record versions and check official version skew. A context name alone is not proof of endpoint identity; the guard also checks the API URL.
sections.example:
Optional cluster setup: follow README.md in order.
Create dedicated kind cluster -> build/load image -> ./lab.ps1 -Action Bootstrap
Then ./lab.ps1 -Action Validate -> ./lab.ps1 -Action Apply
Validate needs the namespace created by Bootstrap.
Offline alternative: python -m unittest -v check_manifests.py

exercise.prompt: Explain what the guard prevents and what it does not prove.
exercise.solution: It blocks accidental operations against a different named or remote endpoint and confines namespace work. It does not certify the local cluster is trusted, guarantee a CNI feature, or replace reviewing the manifests.
checks: Inspect context and endpoint.
Do not mutate an existing shared cluster.

quiz.question: Why explicitly pass --context in lab commands?
options: To select the intended API/identity even if the default changes
To guarantee production isolation from any malicious kubeconfig
quiz.explanation: To select the intended API/identity even if the default changes. It blocks accidental operations against a different named or remote endpoint and confines namespace work. It does not certify the local cluster is trusted, guarantee a CNI feature, or replace reviewing the manifests.

lessons.title: 4. Read manifests, namespaces, labels and selectors
lessons.takeaway: A manifest states apiVersion, kind, metadata and desired fields.

sections.title: Object structure and matching
paragraphs: A manifest states `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata` and desired fields. Names identify objects within a scope; labels classify objects and selectors match label sets. Namespace scope avoids many naming collisions but is not a complete tenant security boundary. The kit uses JSON manifests because Kubernetes accepts JSON as well as YAML; the structures are the same API objects.

sections.title: Selector relationships
paragraphs: Selectors determine which Pods a Service or controller selects. Changing a label can remove a Pod from service routing or controller ownership. Keep controller selectors stable and examine matching Pods/EndpointSlices when diagnosing a Service with no endpoints. The offline checker verifies these specific relationships, not cluster admission.
sections.example:
Deployment selector: app=release-demo
Pod-template label: app=release-demo
Service selector: app=release-demo
All namespaced objects: notebook-lab

sections.title: Try a selector mismatch without a cluster
paragraphs: Make a separate copy of the extracted practice folder. In `workload.json` find the Service object, then change only `spec.selector.app` to `wrong`. Run the single selector test below. It compares the Service selector with the Deployment and template labels, so the altered fixture must fail. Restore `release-demo` and require the check to pass. This tests a local contract; it does not send Kubernetes API requests.
sections.example: python -m unittest -v check_manifests.ManifestChecks.test_selectors_ports_and_security

exercise.prompt: In a practice copy, change only the Service selector to app=wrong and run the named selector test. Predict the failed relationship before running; then restore it. What would the mismatch mean in a live cluster?
exercise.solution: The offline test fails because the Service selector no longer matches the workload labels. Restoring release-demo makes the check pass. A live Service can still exist with that mismatch but has no selected backend for these Pods. Actual endpoints need a separate cluster observation.
checks: Identify the exact Service selector field rather than edit the Pod labels too.
Show failure with the mismatch and success after restoring it.

quiz.question: What causes a selector-based Service to discover these Pods?
quiz.explanation: A selector-based Service discovers Pods whose labels match its selector in the namespace. Readiness and endpoint eligibility still determine usable backends; matching labels alone do not establish application success.

lessons.title: 5. Understand Pod lifetime and shared resources
lessons.takeaway: A Pod is the scheduling unit containing one or more containers with shared networking and selected volumes.

sections.title: Pod identity and shared resources
paragraphs: A Pod is the scheduling unit containing one or more containers with shared networking and selected volumes. Pod instances are disposable; a replacement has a new identity and can run elsewhere. Containers in one Pod communicate through localhost, while different Pods use their assigned network identities or Services. Keep one application container initially, adding sidecars only for a justified shared-lifetime role.

sections.title: Container restart versus Pod replacement
paragraphs: Restarting a container in the same Pod is not the same as replacing the Pod. `emptyDir` survives a container restart within that Pod but disappears when the Pod is removed. The notes demo is intentionally scratch data, so do not claim replacement persistence from a Deployment replica count.
sections.example:
Pod A UID=old → deleted
Replacement Pod B UID=new → new scratch volume
Two containers within B would share network namespace; independent Pods do not share localhost.

exercise.prompt: Predict the lifetime of /tmp data mounted from emptyDir.
exercise.solution: It remains through a container restart in the same Pod, then is lost on Pod removal/replacement. A PVC has a different lifecycle and still needs backup/recovery evidence.
checks: Distinguish container restart from Pod replacement.
Name the volume type.

quiz.question: Which operation ends an emptyDir volume lifetime?
options: Restarting a container within the same Pod
quiz.explanation: Removing the Pod. It remains through a container restart in the same Pod, then is lost on Pod removal/replacement. A PVC has a different lifecycle and still needs backup/recovery evidence.

lessons.title: 6. Reconcile a Deployment instead of hand-managing Pods
lessons.takeaway: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and declarative Pod-template updates.

sections.title: Deployment reconciliation
paragraphs: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets and declarative Pod-template updates. With replicas 2 it aims to keep two desired instances; deleting one managed Pod usually prompts replacement. Editing a standalone Pod is a different contract and does not create a release history. The supplied workload uses apps/v1, a stable selector, bounded revision history and a progress deadline.

sections.title: Availability conditions
paragraphs: A Deployment cannot guarantee availability if nodes lack resources, all images fail or the application is broken. Controller retry is not business-level retry safety. Read desired/current/available replica counts and their conditions before claiming the reconciliation succeeded.
sections.example:
kubectl --context=kind-notebook-lab -n notebook-lab get deploy,rs,pods
# Delete one named lab Pod only after observing ownership.
# Watch a replacement appear with a different name/UID.

exercise.prompt: Why can replicas 2 coexist with availableReplicas 0?
exercise.solution: Desired replicas is a target; both containers may fail image startup or readiness. Inspect ReplicaSet/Pod events, application logs and probes, fix the failure and wait for rollout status rather than increasing replicas blindly.
checks: Compare desired to available replicas.
Inspect owner relationships.

quiz.question: What should replace a deleted managed Pod?
quiz.explanation: The Deployment manages ReplicaSets, whose controllers reconcile the desired Pod count after a managed Pod is deleted. Replacement creation does not guarantee image startup, readiness or correct application state.

lessons.title: 7. Route through Services, DNS and EndpointSlices
lessons.takeaway: A ClusterIP Service gives a stable virtual address and DNS name over matching ready endpoints.

sections.title: Service names and ready endpoints
paragraphs: A ClusterIP Service gives a stable virtual address and DNS name over matching ready endpoints. Its port can differ from the container `targetPort`; a named `targetPort` connects to the container port name. Pod IPs change as instances are replaced. Within `notebook-lab`, `release-demo` resolves the Service, while `release-demo.notebook-lab.svc` identifies its namespace more explicitly.

sections.title: Offline checks versus in-cluster requests
paragraphs: A Service object with no ready matching Pods cannot serve requests. DNS resolution alone also does not prove transport or application health. The local Job exercises actual in-cluster DNS/HTTP only when the learner runs it; the offline checker inspects selector/port consistency.
sections.example:
Job → http://release-demo:8080/version
Service port8080 → targetPort http → containerPort8080
Pod replacement changes endpoint IP; Service name remains.

sections.title: Locate the three port values
paragraphs: In `workload.json`, find the Service port 8080, its `targetPort` string `http`, and the container port named `http` with value 8080. The string is a lookup by name, not another numeric port. An EndpointSlice records backend addresses and readiness for the Service. These records help distinguish a matching label from a backend that can actually receive traffic.

exercise.prompt: Troubleshoot a successful DNS lookup followed by connection failure.
exercise.solution: Inspect Service port/targetPort, selector, EndpointSlices, readiness and policy enforcement in that order. Separate name resolution from usable ready backends and application HTTP results.
checks: Check endpoints and readiness.
Distinguish DNS from transport.

quiz.question: Which name is stable across ordinary Pod replacement?
quiz.explanation: The Service name remains stable while backing Pods are replaced. Clients still need working resolution, eligible endpoints, connectivity and an application response.

lessons.title: 8. Configure behavior with a ConfigMap
lessons.takeaway: A ConfigMap carries non-confidential configuration separately from container bytes.

sections.title: Configuration delivery
paragraphs: A ConfigMap stores non-confidential configuration outside the container image. The kit injects `RELEASE_VERSION` through `envFrom`. This value is a release label, not a hash of the deployed bytes. The container reads environment variables when it starts. Editing the ConfigMap does not change the environment of an already running process.

sections.title: Mounted files and process reload
paragraphs: Mounted configuration files have different update behavior and applications still must reload them appropriately; `subPath` mounts do not receive normal ConfigMap updates. Avoid assuming every configuration delivery method has the same lifecycle. Record config revision with the release image.
sections.example:
release-config: RELEASE_VERSION=v1
Pod environment captures v1 at startup
ConfigMap becomes v2 → existing process still reports v1
Controlled rollout creates new Pods with new environment.

exercise.prompt: Predict /version after editing only the ConfigMap data.
exercise.solution: Existing environment-injected Pods keep v1. Restart the intended workload through a controlled rollout and observe new process values; do not relabel this as proof the image changed.
checks: Distinguish config update from Pod restart.
Separate release label from digest.

quiz.question: When does an envFrom ConfigMap change reach an existing process?
options: After a new/restarted container receives its environment
quiz.explanation: After a new/restarted container receives its environment. Existing environment-injected Pods keep v1. Restart the intended workload through a controlled rollout and observe new process values; do not relabel this as proof the image changed.

lessons.title: 9. Treat Secrets as protected references, not encryption
lessons.takeaway: A Kubernetes Secret separates confidential configuration from ordinary application manifests, but base64 encoding is not encryption.

sections.title: Secret representation and protection
paragraphs: A Kubernetes Secret separates confidential configuration from ordinary application manifests, but base64 encoding is not encryption. Protection depends on storage encryption, access controls, workloads and the system that supplies/rotates the value. The download contains an unmistakable fake demo token in a separate manifest that is not required for the baseline workload. Never put real credentials in the practice bundle or Git history.

sections.title: Indirect access and rotation
paragraphs: Anyone able to create a Pod that mounts a Secret may be able to obtain it even without direct get-secret permission. Review indirect access and namespace trust. Environment-injected secret changes need process lifecycle handling; do not assume a value rotates automatically inside existing processes.
sections.example:
demo-secret.json: fake-only-not-a-credential
Runtime service account: automountServiceAccountToken=false
Real environment: secret store → restricted runtime reference

exercise.prompt: Explain why base64 in a committed Secret is not adequate protection.
exercise.solution: The value is readily decoded and persists in history. Keep real values outside the public repository, control direct and workload-mediated access, configure at-rest protection and rehearse rotation without logging the credential.
checks: Discuss indirect Pod access.
Keep the sample fake.

quiz.question: What does base64 encoding provide?
options: An encoding reversible without a secret key
quiz.explanation: An encoding reversible without a secret key. The value is readily decoded and persists in history. Keep real values outside the public repository, control direct and workload-mediated access, configure at-rest protection and rehearse rotation without logging the credential.

lessons.title: 10. Design startup, readiness and liveness independently
lessons.takeaway: Startup probes give initialization time before liveness/readiness checks run.

sections.title: Independent health probes
paragraphs: Startup probes give initialization time before liveness/readiness checks run. Readiness controls eligible service traffic; liveness can restart a failing container. The kit uses /live for startup/liveness and /ready for required local schema/gate readiness. This avoids turning one dependency outage into repeated process restarts. Probe thresholds must match observed startup and recovery behavior rather than copied defaults.

sections.title: Probe timing and local evidence
paragraphs: Timing also depends on scheduling and probe execution; the arithmetic is an approximate configured budget, not an SLA. An aggressive liveness check on a shared dependency can worsen an outage. The local HTTP test confirms that /ready can return 503 while /live returns 200. It does not exercise kubelet probe scheduling.
sections.example:
startup /live: period5s × failureThreshold12≈60s failure budget
readiness /ready: failure removes ready eligibility
liveness /live: repeated failure triggers container restart

sections.title: Follow one failing Pod into the Service endpoints
paragraphs: Two replicas are Ready. Creating /tmp/not-ready in one replica makes /ready return 503 while /live still returns 200. The kubelet eventually marks that Pod unready; the EndpointSlice controller updates its ready condition. The Pod can remain Running with the same UID and restart count. Traffic selection changes because readiness changed, not because the process died.

Run the optional `readiness_drill.py` only after the existing kind lab is healthy. It guards the named loopback context and namespace ownership, changes one Pod, checks its EndpointSlice and restores its gate in `finally`. Transitions are asynchronous, so it polls conditions with deadlines rather than assuming an immediate update. A long-lived connection already attached to the Pod is a separate boundary; endpoint readiness is not proof that every existing connection vanished.
sections.example:
before: Ready=True, restartCount=N
gate present: Ready=False, endpoint.ready=False, restartCount=N
gate removed: Ready=True, restartCount=N

exercise.prompt: Run the optional probe drill, or trace its checks. If the restart count increases while only the readiness gate changed, which evidence contradicts the intended probe design?
checks: The chosen Pod UID remains stable and its endpoint readiness becomes false.
Restarts remain unchanged through gate creation and recovery; an increase triggers inspection of liveness/events, not a success claim.
exercise.solution: Readiness should change traffic eligibility without restarting this service. A restart requires another cause: inspect container termination reason, events and actual startup/liveness paths. Keep Pod UID in the record so a replacement Pod is not mistaken for recovery of the same process. The script removes its own gate even if an assertion fails.

quiz.question: Which probe should normally represent temporary inability to serve work?
options: Liveness that fails whenever a shared dependency is unavailable
Startup checks alone after initialization has finished
quiz.explanation: Readiness. /ready becomes503 so readiness eventually fails; /live remains200 so this condition should not cause a liveness restart. Remove the file and inspect readiness recovery. Record actual thresholds/timestamps during the optional drill.

lessons.title: 11. Use requests for scheduling and limits for runtime boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Resource requests inform scheduling and some utilization calculations; limits constrain runtime usage differently for CPU and memory.

sections.title: Scheduling requests and runtime limits
paragraphs: Resource requests inform scheduling and some utilization calculations; limits constrain runtime usage differently for CPU and memory. CPU over a limit can be throttled, while excessive memory can lead to termination. The lab requests 100m CPU and 64 Mi of memory, with limits of 500m CPU and 128 Mi of memory. These are teaching values, not measured capacity recommendations. Observe actual usage before tuning or adding autoscaling.

sections.title: CPU units and HPA inputs
paragraphs: Scheduling considers requests and additional placement conditions, not only current CPU percentage. One hundred millicores is 0.1 core. For CPU utilization HPA, missing requests can prevent a useful percentage calculation; arbitrary low requests can distort scaling signals.
sections.example:
Node free requested capacity: 200m CPU
Pod request: 300m → may remain Pending
Running Pod: CPU limit 500m → throttling possible
Memory beyond limit 128Mi → OOM risk

exercise.prompt: A Pending Pod uses no CPU. Why can its CPU request still be the cause?
exercise.solution: The scheduler reserves against requested capacity and cannot fit the declared request, even when measured instantaneous usage appears low. Inspect FailedScheduling events and node allocatable/request totals before reducing values.
checks: Use correct units.
Separate requested capacity from observed use.
hints: The scheduler places a Pod by its request, before it has used anything.
Compare the request with what the node still has unrequested, not with what it is using.
pitfalls: Reading node CPU usage instead of requested totals.

quiz.question: What is 100m CPU?
quiz.explanation: 100m is one tenth of a CPU core. Requests influence scheduling and resource allocation; this notation does not itself describe the application's measured CPU use.

references.title: Resource management
references.section: Requests and limits; scheduling and resource limits
references.scope: Stable Kubernetes API concepts. Optional cluster execution and its recorded results are described in the practice guide.

practice.prompt: A node has 2,000m allocatable CPU, and Pods already on it request 1,400m. A Deployment of 3 replicas requests 250m each. Finish the fit calculation: how many replicas can the scheduler place there, and what happens to the rest?
hints: Work in millicores throughout.
practice.solution: Unrequested capacity is 2,000m − 1,400m = 600m. Each replica needs 250m, so 2 fit, using 500m; the third would need 750m in total and stays Pending with a FailedScheduling event, even if the node's measured CPU is mostly idle. Fix it with another node or a justified smaller request, not by guessing.
checks: Subtracts requested, not used, CPU.
Shows how many replicas fit and why.
Names the Pending state and the event to check.

practice.prompt: One container has a 500m CPU limit and needs 700m during a burst. Another has a 128Mi memory limit and grows to 150Mi. What happens to each?
hints: Can the kernel take memory back from a process the way it can delay CPU time?
practice.solution: The CPU-bound container is throttled to 500m, half a core: it slows down but keeps running. The memory-bound container is killed for exceeding its limit (OOMKilled, exit code 137) and restarted by the kubelet. CPU is compressible and memory is not, so a memory limit set too low shows up as restarts, not slowness.
checks: Throttles CPU.
Kills the container on memory overrun.
Explains compressible versus incompressible resources.

practice.prompt: An HPA targets 70% average CPU utilization. Each Pod requests 100m and 2 replicas average 140m. How many replicas does the HPA ask for, and what would change if the request were 200m?
hints: The HPA scales by current utilization divided by target utilization.
practice.solution: Utilization is usage over request: 140 / 100 = 140%. Desired replicas = ceil(2 × 140 / 70) = 4. With a 200m request the same usage is 70%, exactly on target, so it stays at 2. The request is the denominator of the scaling signal, so an arbitrary request distorts scaling.
checks: Computes utilization against the request.
Applies the HPA formula with rounding up.
Shows how the request changes the outcome.

practice.prompt: For a latency-sensitive API, a teammate proposes setting requests equal to limits for CPU and memory. When is that the right call?
hints: What does the node reserve, and what happens during a spike above it?
practice.solution: It gives the Pod the Guaranteed QoS class, so it is evicted last under node pressure and gets predictable resources. The cost is reserved capacity that sits idle between bursts, and CPU throttling at the limit during spikes. It suits critical, steady services; bursty or batch workloads usually do better with requests below limits.
checks: Names the Guaranteed QoS class.
States the idle-capacity and throttling cost.
Says which workloads it suits.

lessons.title: 12. Roll a compatible Pod template and diagnose stalls
lessons.takeaway: A Deployment rollout changes the Pod template, creates a new ReplicaSet and transitions availability according to maxSurge/maxUnavailable.

sections.title: Rollout capacity and deadlines
paragraphs: A Deployment rollout changes the Pod template, creates a new ReplicaSet and transitions availability according to `maxSurge`/`maxUnavailable`. For two replicas, the kit sets `maxSurge` to 1 and `maxUnavailable` to 0. This requires spare capacity for a third replica during rollout. A progress deadline signals a stalled rollout but does not automatically undo it. Application/data compatibility remains a separate release gate.

sections.title: Loading a distinct local image
paragraphs: Changing a label in the ConfigMap alone is not a Pod-template change. For the local drill update the Deployment image to a separately built local v2 image, load that image into kind and watch status. Returning to the old image is safe only for the supplied unchanged-schema simulation.
sections.example:
2 old +1 surge candidate
Candidate Ready → reduce old
Repeat until2 new
Candidate never Ready → rollout waits/fails progress condition

exercise.prompt: Predict a rollout with no spare schedulable capacity.
exercise.solution: With unavailable 0 and surge 1, a new Pod may stay Pending while the two old Pods remain. Add justified capacity or revise the reviewed rollout budget; do not disable readiness just to make the status green.
checks: Explain spare capacity.
Keep readiness as a real gate.
hints: With `maxUnavailable: 0`, an old Pod is removed only after a new one is Ready.
Where would the extra, surge Pod run?
pitfalls: Disabling readiness to make a stuck rollout look healthy.
Expecting a progress deadline to roll back automatically.

quiz.question: Does progressDeadlineSeconds automatically perform rollback?
options: No; it reports progress failure for a release controller/operator to handle
quiz.explanation: progressDeadlineSeconds makes stalled progress visible through Deployment status. It does not automatically revert the release; a release controller or operator must decide and perform recovery.

practice.prompt: A Deployment has 4 replicas with `maxSurge: 25%` and `maxUnavailable: 25%`. Kubernetes rounds surge up and unavailable down. Finish the bounds: the most Pods that can exist and the fewest that must stay available during the rollout.
hints: Compute both percentages of 4 first, then round.
practice.solution: Surge is 25% of 4 = 1, so at most 5 Pods exist. Unavailable is 25% of 4 = 1, so at least 3 must stay available. The rollout can start a new Pod and stop an old one at the same time, so it needs room for one extra Pod.
checks: Applies the percentages to the replica count.
Gives the upper and lower bounds.

practice.prompt: Same percentages, 10 replicas. What are the bounds now?
hints: Which direction does each value round?
practice.solution: 25% of 10 is 2.5. Surge rounds up to 3, so at most 13 Pods exist. Unavailable rounds down to 2, so at least 8 stay available. Rounding favours availability in both directions: more room to add, less allowed to remove.
checks: Rounds surge up and unavailable down.
Gives both bounds.
pitfalls: Rounding both values the same way.

practice.prompt: Version 2 reads a new database column, and version 1 crashes if that column contains NULL. During the rollout both versions run at once. How do you release the schema and code safely?
hints: Which Pods are reading the database halfway through the rollout?
practice.solution: Expand, then contract. First add the column so that version 1 still works, for example with a default and no NULLs it cannot handle. Then roll out version 2. Only when no version 1 Pods remain, and rollback to it is no longer needed, tighten or remove what version 1 depended on. A rolling update guarantees mixed versions, so every step must work with both.
checks: Recognises that both versions run together.
Orders the schema and code changes as expand and contract.
Keeps rollback possible.

practice.prompt: A rollout passed its `progressDeadlineSeconds` and the Deployment reports `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`. Should you wait for Kubernetes to roll it back?
hints: What does the condition change on its own?
practice.solution: No. The condition only reports the stall; Kubernetes does not undo the rollout. Diagnose first: events, the new Pods' readiness and logs, and scheduling. Then run `kubectl rollout undo` or fix forward. Automated rollback needs a separate tool or pipeline step that watches this condition.
checks: States what Kubernetes does on its own.
Diagnoses before undoing.
Names `kubectl rollout undo`.

lessons.title: 13. Explain affinity, topology and taints before pinning
lessons.takeaway: Scheduling combines resource fit with placement constraints.

sections.title: Placement constraints
paragraphs: Scheduling combines resource fit with placement constraints. Node selectors/affinity express placement needs, topology spread can reduce concentration, and taints repel Pods unless tolerated. A toleration permits consideration; it does not force assignment to that node. Begin with unconstrained placement in the small local cluster and add a constraint only when you can identify its operational purpose.

sections.title: Single-node limitations
paragraphs: The baseline deliberately omits hard multi-zone rules because a single-node kind cluster cannot satisfy them meaningfully. A workload pinned to one node loses resilience on that node failure. Inspect labels/taints/events, and distinguish availability goals from hardware/security placement requirements.
sections.example:
Node label: workload=demo
required nodeAffinity: workload=demo → only matching nodes
Taint dedicated=ops:NoSchedule → needs matching toleration
No matching capacity → Pending

exercise.prompt: Does adding a toleration guarantee placement on the tainted node?
exercise.solution: No: the scheduler can consider that node but other constraints and scoring still apply. Combine a justified node affinity with toleration when dedicated placement is required, and test capacity/failure consequences.
checks: Distinguish permission from preference/requirement.
Explain single-node limitations.
hints: A taint keeps Pods away; a toleration only removes that barrier.
Which constraint actually says 'this node'?
pitfalls: Assuming a toleration attracts a Pod to a node.
Pinning workloads to one node and losing resilience.

quiz.question: A toleration alone does what?
options: Allows consideration despite a matching taint
quiz.explanation: A matching toleration permits the scheduler to consider a tainted node. It neither requires placement there nor overrides resource, affinity and other scheduling constraints.

references.title: Taints and tolerations
references.scope: Stable Kubernetes API concepts. Optional cluster execution and its recorded results are described in the practice guide.

practice.prompt: Node A has label `workload=demo` and taint `dedicated=ops:NoSchedule`. Node B has label `workload=demo` and no taint. A Pod has required affinity `workload=demo` and a toleration for `dedicated=ops`. Finish the table: which nodes may the Pod land on, and what would make it land only on node A?
hints: Check each node against the affinity, then against the taint.
practice.solution: Both nodes match the affinity, and the toleration allows node A, so the Pod may land on either; scoring decides. To require node A, give A a label that B lacks, such as `dedicated=ops`, and require it in node affinity alongside the toleration. The taint keeps other Pods off A; the affinity keeps this Pod on it.
checks: Checks each node against both constraints.
Combines a unique label in affinity with the toleration.

practice.prompt: A Deployment of 3 replicas uses topology spread with `maxSkew: 1` across zones `a` and `b`, with `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`. How can the replicas be spread, and what happens if zone `b` has no capacity?
hints: Skew is the largest count minus the smallest count.
practice.solution: The difference between zones may be at most 1, so the spread is 2 and 1, in either zone. If zone `b` is full, putting all three in `a` would make the skew 3, so the third replica that cannot keep the skew stays Pending. With `ScheduleAnyway` it would be placed anyway, trading even spread for availability.
checks: Gives the possible spread.
States that the unsatisfiable replica stays Pending.
Contrasts `ScheduleAnyway`.

practice.prompt: Three replicas use required pod anti-affinity on `kubernetes.io/hostname`, so no two share a node. The cluster has 2 nodes. What happens, and what softer option exists?
hints: How many nodes have no replica yet when the third is scheduled?
practice.solution: Two replicas run on separate nodes and the third stays Pending, because every node already holds one. Preferred anti-affinity, or topology spread with `ScheduleAnyway`, would place the third on a node that already has one while still spreading when possible. Use required anti-affinity only when sharing a node is truly unacceptable.
checks: States what happens to each replica.
Offers preferred anti-affinity or a soft spread.

practice.prompt: To make a database Pod 'stable', a teammate sets `nodeName` to one specific node. Is that a good idea?
hints: What happens to this Pod if that node is drained?
practice.solution: No. `nodeName` bypasses the scheduler, so resource checks and constraints are skipped, and if that node fails the Pod cannot move. Express the real need instead: node affinity for the storage or hardware it requires, and a StatefulSet with persistent volumes for stable identity and data.
checks: Explains that `nodeName` bypasses the scheduler.
Names the loss of failover.
Proposes affinity and a StatefulSet.

lessons.title: 14. Test allowed and denied traffic with an enforcing CNI
lessons.takeaway: NetworkPolicy selects Pods and declares allowed ingress/egress connections.

sections.title: Traffic policy and enforcement
paragraphs: NetworkPolicy selects Pods and declares allowed ingress/egress connections. A policy object can be accepted without enforcement if the cluster network plugin does not implement it. The optional lab policy isolates ingress to `app=release-demo` and permits port 8080 only from same-namespace `app=notebook-client` Pods. Baseline kind networking does not by itself establish policy enforcement.

sections.title: Allowed and denied clients
paragraphs: Pod/namespace selector combination changes scope; separate list entries can be alternatives while selectors in the same peer are combined. Network policy is not HTTP authentication or TLS. Before claiming denial, run both an allowed client and an unlabelled client and verify the plugin; a refused service with no endpoints is a different failure.
sections.example:
app-ingress selects release-demo
Allowed: notebook-client → TCP 8080
Denied: other Pod → TCP 8080, if CNI enforces policy
Egress is unchanged because policyTypes lists Ingress only.

exercise.prompt: A deny policy is present but an unlabelled client succeeds. What next? Optional live cluster track: practice/optional-enforcement-track.md; document prerequisites and actual positive/negative results.
exercise.solution: Confirm target labels, policy namespace/semantics and CNI enforcement. Do not mark isolation passed because kubectl apply succeeded. Use a compatible enforcing local CNI as a separately reviewed optional setup before repeating the paired traffic checks.
checks: Verify enforcement prerequisites.
Run allowed and denied probes.
hints: Check three things separately: the labels, the policy's meaning and whether the network plugin enforces policies at all.
A single successful probe proves nothing; you need an allowed one and a denied one.
pitfalls: Calling isolation tested because `kubectl apply` succeeded.
Confusing a Service with no endpoints with a denied connection.

quiz.question: Which claim is valid after apply alone?
options: The API accepted the policy object
quiz.explanation: The API accepted the policy object. Confirm target labels, policy namespace/semantics and CNI enforcement. Do not mark isolation passed because kubectl apply succeeded. Use a compatible enforcing local CNI as a separately reviewed optional setup before repeating the paired traffic checks.

references.title: Network policies
references.scope: Stable Kubernetes API concepts. Optional cluster execution and its recorded results are described in the practice guide.

practice.prompt: The policy for `release-demo` must also allow Prometheus in namespace `monitoring`. Two drafts: (1) one `from` entry with both `namespaceSelector: monitoring` and `podSelector: app=prometheus`; (2) two separate entries, one with each selector. Pods: `prometheus` and `grafana` in `monitoring`, and a `prometheus`-labelled debug Pod in `notebook-lab`. Which Pods does each draft allow?
hints: A `podSelector` alone selects Pods in the policy's own namespace.
practice.solution: Draft 1 combines the selectors, so it allows only the `prometheus` Pod in `monitoring`. Draft 2 lists alternatives: every Pod in `monitoring`, including `grafana`, plus any Pod in the policy's own namespace labelled `app=prometheus`, including the debug Pod. Draft 1 is what was intended; one extra dash turns AND into OR.
checks: Treats selectors in one entry as AND.
Treats separate entries as OR.
Lists the allowed Pods for each draft.

practice.prompt: You add an Egress policy type with no egress rules to `release-demo`, to block outbound traffic. Its calls to an in-cluster service by name now fail. Why, and what rule do you add?
hints: What does the Pod do before it can connect to a service name?
practice.solution: Declaring Egress with no rules denies all outbound traffic, including DNS lookups to the cluster DNS service, so names no longer resolve. Add an egress rule allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to the DNS Pods in `kube-system`, then rules for each service it must reach.
checks: Identifies DNS as the first thing blocked.
Allows port 53 to the cluster DNS Pods.

practice.prompt: A team asks whether NetworkPolicy can ensure that only the `orders` service may call `POST /refunds` on `payments`. Can it?
hints: What does a NetworkPolicy rule match on?
practice.solution: Only partly. NetworkPolicy works at layers 3 and 4: it can allow traffic from `orders` Pods to the `payments` port, but it cannot see HTTP methods or paths, or verify who is calling. Combine it with authentication between services, for example mTLS identities from a service mesh, and authorization in `payments` for the specific operation.
checks: States that NetworkPolicy cannot see HTTP methods or paths.
Adds service identity and application authorization.

practice.prompt: On a default kind cluster, the denied client still connects after you apply the policy. A teammate wants to mark the isolation test as passed because 'the policy is correct'. Should you?
hints: Which component is responsible for enforcing the policy?
practice.solution: No. The test shows that nothing enforced the policy; the default kind network plugin does not implement NetworkPolicy. Record the result as not enforced, and either install an enforcing plugin for the optional track or state that isolation is untested. A policy that is not enforced protects nothing.
checks: Records the actual result.
Names plugin enforcement as the missing piece.

lessons.title: 15. Bring outside traffic in with Ingress and the Gateway API
lessons.takeaway: A controller implements HTTP routing into the cluster; Ingress is the older, simpler API, and the Gateway API separates infrastructure ownership from application routes.

sections.title: From the edge to a Service
paragraphs: A ClusterIP Service (lesson 7) is reachable only inside the cluster. A `LoadBalancer` Service asks the cloud for an external layer 4 load balancer per Service, which is simple but costly and has no HTTP routing. For HTTP, one shared entry point routes by host name and path to many Services, and terminates TLS once.

An Ingress object declares those rules, and an ingress controller (a reverse proxy running in the cluster) implements them. Without a controller, an Ingress does nothing. Its API covers host, path and TLS; anything else, such as header matching, traffic splitting or timeouts, is expressed in controller-specific annotations, so manifests stop being portable.

The Gateway API is the newer, more expressive successor. A GatewayClass names an implementation, a Gateway declares listeners (ports, protocols, host names and certificates) and usually belongs to a platform team, and HTTPRoutes attached to it belong to application teams in their own namespaces. Matching on headers, weighted backends for canary releases and cross-namespace permissions are part of the standard API.
sections.example:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: public
  namespace: edge                  # owned by the platform team
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example-lb
  listeners:
  - name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
    port: 443
    hostname: "*.example.test"
    tls:
      mode: Terminate
      certificateRefs: [{name: wildcard-example-test}]
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces: {from: All}
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: notebook
  namespace: notebook-lab          # owned by the application team
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: public, namespace: edge}]
  hostnames: ["notebook.example.test"]
  rules:
  - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /api}}]
    backendRefs: [{name: release-demo, port: 8080}]
  - backendRefs: [{name: web, port: 80}]

sections.title: TLS and ownership
paragraphs: The Gateway terminates TLS with a certificate stored as a Secret (lesson 9), usually issued and renewed automatically by a tool such as cert-manager. Traffic from the Gateway to the Pods is then plain HTTP inside the cluster unless you add mutual TLS. The listener's `allowedRoutes` decides which namespaces may attach routes, so one team cannot take over another's host name.

The manifests were checked offline: the route's parent reference matches the Gateway's name and namespace, and its host name falls under the listener's wildcard. They were not applied to a cluster, and `example-lb` stands for whichever GatewayClass your cluster provides.

exercise.prompt: Two teams share a cluster. Team A serves shop.example.test, team B serves blog.example.test, and both need HTTPS. Describe how you would split the Gateway API objects between the platform team and the two application teams, and what stops team B from routing shop.example.test.
exercise.solution: The platform team owns the GatewayClass and one Gateway in an edge namespace, with an HTTPS listener for each host name (or a wildcard) and the certificates. Each application team creates an HTTPRoute in its own namespace with a parentRef to that Gateway and its own host name. To stop team B claiming shop.example.test, give each host its own listener and restrict allowedRoutes for that listener to team A's namespace (with a namespace selector), so a route from team B's namespace cannot attach to it.
checks: Platform team owns Gateway, listeners and certificates.
Application teams own their route objects in their own namespaces.
Uses allowedRoutes to restrict which namespaces attach to which listener.
hints: Separate the shared parts, entry point and certificates, from what each team changes.
Which object decides which namespaces may attach routes to a listener?
pitfalls: Letting every namespace attach routes to every listener.
Assuming traffic behind the Gateway is encrypted.

quiz.question: An Ingress object is created in a cluster that has no ingress controller installed. What happens?
options: Kubernetes creates a default load balancer
Nothing routes traffic; the object is stored but not implemented
The API server rejects the object
quiz.explanation: Ingress and Gateway objects are declarations. A controller must watch them and configure a proxy.

practice.prompt: Using the lesson's `notebook` HTTPRoute, finish the routing table: where do requests for `notebook.example.test/api/orders`, `notebook.example.test/about` and `blog.example.test/api` go?
hints: Host names are checked before paths.
practice.solution: `/api/orders` matches the `/api` prefix rule and goes to `release-demo` on port 8080. `/about` matches no path rule, so it falls to the rule with no match and goes to `web` on port 80. `blog.example.test` is not in the route's host names, so this route does not handle it; unless another route claims it, the Gateway returns 404.
checks: Matches the path prefix.
Uses the fallback rule.
Checks the host name first.

practice.prompt: For a canary, the `/api` rule gets two backends: `release-demo` with weight 90 and `release-demo-v2` with weight 10. About how many of 1,000 API requests reach v2, and what should you watch?
hints: The share is one weight divided by the sum of the weights.
practice.solution: About 100, a tenth of the requests: 10 / (90 + 10). Each request is assigned independently, so the actual number varies a little. Compare v2's error rate and latency with v1's over the same period before raising its weight, and keep the change reversible by editing the weights back.
checks: Computes the share from the weights.
Compares v2 with v1 before increasing the weight.

practice.prompt: A cluster exposes 12 HTTP services, each as a `LoadBalancer` Service. What does that cost compared with one Gateway, and when is a `LoadBalancer` Service still the right choice?
hints: What does each `LoadBalancer` Service ask the cloud provider to create?
practice.solution: Twelve cloud load balancers, each billed and each with its own address and certificate handling, and no host or path routing. One Gateway gives a single entry point, TLS terminated once and routing to all twelve. A `LoadBalancer` Service still fits non-HTTP protocols or a single service that needs its own layer 4 entry point.
checks: Counts the load balancers and their costs.
Says when layer 4 exposure still fits.

practice.prompt: A team needs to expose an MQTT broker on TCP port 8883. Should they write an Ingress for it?
hints: Which protocols does the Ingress API describe?
practice.solution: No. Ingress routes HTTP and HTTPS only. Use a `LoadBalancer` Service, or a Gateway with a TCP or TLS listener and a TCPRoute or TLSRoute if the chosen implementation supports them. Check which route types your GatewayClass implements.
checks: Recognises that Ingress is HTTP only.
Names a layer 4 option.

lessons.title: 16. Separate identities and scope RBAC permissions
lessons.takeaway: Authentication establishes an API identity; RBAC authorization permits verbs on resources within scope.

sections.title: RBAC identities and scope
paragraphs: Authentication establishes an API identity; RBAC authorization permits verbs on resources within scope. A Role is namespaced, a ClusterRole can express cluster-wide resource rules or be bound within a namespace, and bindings connect subjects to rules. The optional viewer role grants read/list/watch on Pods and Pod logs in notebook-lab; the runtime workload has no auto-mounted API token.

sections.title: Impersonation and denied operations
paragraphs: Impersonation-based `kubectl auth can-i` checks require an identity allowed to impersonate and do not prove the application identity provider. Avoid broad wildcards and unintended escalation through workload creation. Explicitly verify a permitted read and a denied secret/mutation operation in the dedicated local namespace.
sections.example:
viewer ServiceAccount → RoleBinding → pod-viewer Role
Allowed: get/list/watch pods and pods/log
Not granted: read secrets, create Pods, mutating Deployments

exercise.prompt: Would a Role granting create Pods be safe just because it excludes get Secrets?
exercise.solution: Not necessarily: created Pods can mount namespace Secrets or powerful service accounts. Review indirect access/escalation, constrain workload/admission permissions and keep the viewer limited to required observations.
checks: Include subresource and namespace scope.
Explain indirect escalation.
hints: Creating a Pod lets you choose what that Pod mounts and which service account it runs as.
Think about what you could read from inside a Pod you created.
pitfalls: Judging a Role only by the resources it names directly.

quiz.question: What does a namespaced RoleBinding determine?
options: Which subjects receive referenced rules in that namespace
quiz.explanation: A namespaced RoleBinding grants its subjects the referenced Role or ClusterRole rules within that namespace. Effective access also depends on the actual rules and indirect privileges, such as creating workloads that use Secrets or service accounts.

references.title: RBAC authorization
references.section: Role and ClusterRole; RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding
references.scope: Stable Kubernetes API concepts. Optional cluster execution and its recorded results are described in the practice guide.

practice.prompt: Using the lesson's `pod-viewer` Role, finish the table for the `viewer` service account: can it `get pods/log`, `delete pods` and `get secrets` in `notebook-lab`?
hints: Read the Role's rules: resources and verbs.
practice.solution: `get pods/log`: yes, so `kubectl logs` works. `delete pods`: no, the Role grants only get, list and watch. `get secrets`: no, Secrets are not listed. Subresources such as `pods/log` must be named explicitly; granting `pods` alone would not allow reading logs.
checks: Checks each verb against each resource.
Notes that subresources are granted separately.

practice.prompt: The rules are moved into a ClusterRole. What can `viewer` read if it is bound with a RoleBinding in `notebook-lab`, and what if it is bound with a ClusterRoleBinding?
hints: Which object decides where the rules apply?
practice.solution: With a RoleBinding the permissions apply only in `notebook-lab`, even though the rules live in a ClusterRole; this is how one ClusterRole is reused across namespaces. With a ClusterRoleBinding, `viewer` can read Pods and logs in every namespace. The binding, not the role, sets the scope.
checks: Scopes a RoleBinding to its namespace.
Scopes a ClusterRoleBinding to the whole cluster.

practice.prompt: A CI service account may `create` and `update` Deployments in `notebook-lab`, but nothing about Secrets. What can it indirectly access, and how would you limit that?
hints: What can a Pod template mount?
practice.solution: A Deployment creates Pods, and a Pod template can mount any Secret in the namespace or run as any service account there, so the CI account can read Secrets and borrow other accounts' permissions. Limit it with Pod Security admission, a policy engine that restricts mounts and service accounts, a namespace containing only what the workload needs, and reviewed manifests.
checks: Explains escalation through Pod templates.
Proposes admission controls or namespace isolation.

practice.prompt: The deploy pipeline fails with 'forbidden' and someone proposes binding it to `cluster-admin` to unblock the release. Should you?
hints: The error message names the exact verb and resource.
practice.solution: No. `cluster-admin` grants everything in every namespace, so a leaked pipeline token would control the whole cluster. Read the denied verb and resource from the error, grant that in a namespaced Role, and check it with `kubectl auth can-i`. Fix the permission, not the symptom.
checks: Weighs the blast radius of the proposed binding.
Grants the specific denied permission in a namespace.
Verifies with `kubectl auth can-i`.

lessons.title: 17. Harden a workload and distinguish admission from runtime
lessons.takeaway: Pod security settings restrict process privileges and filesystem capabilities.

sections.title: Process privileges and filesystems
paragraphs: Pod security settings restrict process privileges and filesystem capabilities. The baseline runs as non-root user 10001, disables privilege escalation, drops Linux capabilities, uses `RuntimeDefault` seccomp and a read-only root filesystem. A writable `emptyDir` at `/tmp` supports this application. The namespace requests restricted Pod Security admission at v1.34, independently of the application configuration.

sections.title: Admission versus runtime evidence
paragraphs: Admission controls decide whether the Pod specification is allowed; they do not prove the base image has no vulnerabilities or that business authorization works. The baseline has no `hostPath`, privileged container or external load balancer. Read-only root needs compatible temp/cache/data paths and should be tested with the actual image.
sections.example:
USER 10001 + runAsNonRoot
allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
capabilities drop ALL
readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
/tmp is an explicit writable volume

exercise.prompt: Why does the app need a writable /tmp mount under a read-only root?
exercise.solution: Its local SQLite file and temporary state must live on an explicitly writable volume. Keep /app read-only, use least privilege, and verify permissions as the numeric runtime user instead of switching the whole container back to root.
checks: Explain required writable paths.
Separate image risk from Pod privilege.

quiz.question: Which setting directly removes Linux capabilities?
quiz.explanation: capabilities.drop: [ALL] removes Linux capabilities from the container. Non-root execution, writable-path permissions and filesystem restrictions are separate controls and must be tested together.

lessons.title: 18. Connect PVC lifecycle, access mode and recovery
lessons.takeaway: A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage supplied by a matching volume or StorageClass.

sections.title: Claims, access modes and reclaim
paragraphs: A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage supplied by a matching volume or StorageClass. A Pod mounts the claim; deleting a Pod need not delete the claim/data, while deleting the claim can trigger provider-specific reclaim behavior. ReadWriteOnce means read-write mounting by a single node, not a universal one-Pod distributed lock. The optional storage-demo writes one synthetic file to a dedicated claim.

sections.title: Provisioning and driver permissions
paragraphs: Provisioning may wait for first consumer or stay `Pending` if no default StorageClass exists. A PVC with local-node backing is not multi-node failover or an off-node backup. `fsGroup` support and ownership depend on the driver; inspect events if the non-root writer cannot open `/data`.
sections.example:
storage.json → PVC lab-data +Pod storage-demo
Delete storage-demo only → reapply → same message if storage remains
Delete namespace/PVC → data may be deleted by reclaim policy

exercise.prompt: Does a bound PVC prove disaster recoverability? Optional live cluster track: practice/optional-enforcement-track.md; document prerequisites and actual positive/negative results.
exercise.solution: No: verify access permissions, actual retained data after Pod replacement, backend/reclaim behavior and independent backups. A disk or cluster loss can remove the only copy even when the claim remains in API state.
checks: Inspect StorageClass and reclaim policy.
Test retained contents separately from backup.

quiz.question: ReadWriteOnce is best interpreted as?
quiz.explanation: ReadWriteOnce describes read-write mounting from one node. It does not mean one Pod, guarantee durable retention, or establish backup and recovery.

lessons.title: 19. Run finite Jobs with bounded retries and idempotent work
lessons.takeaway: A Job manages work intended to finish, unlike a continuously serving Deployment.

sections.title: Finite work and retry bounds
paragraphs: A Job manages work intended to finish, unlike a continuously serving Deployment. Set completion behavior, retry bounds and a deadline. The lab Job requests `/version` through Service DNS, prints the result and exits; `backoffLimit` 1 and `activeDeadlineSeconds` 60 bound retries/time. Jobs can still run work more than once due to failure/replacement, so external effects require idempotency.

sections.title: Migration ownership and log retention
paragraphs: The supplied Job has no irreversible side effects. Do not run database migrations independently in every API Pod as a substitute for a reviewed migration job. Cleanup TTL means logs may disappear; capture evidence before it expires. Changing an existing Job template normally requires a new Job identity.
sections.example:
batch/v1 Job version-check
restartPolicy:Never
backoffLimit:1
activeDeadlineSeconds:60
ttlSecondsAfterFinished:300

exercise.prompt: A payment Job times out after the external provider commits. What should retry do?
exercise.solution: Use a durable scoped idempotency key and reconcile uncertain outcomes; another Pod execution must not create another payment. A Job controller completion guarantee is not an exactly-once business-effect guarantee.
checks: Bound retry and deadline.
Preserve uncertain-outcome semantics.

quiz.question: What does backoffLimit fail to guarantee?
quiz.explanation: Exactly one external side effect. Use a durable scoped idempotency key and reconcile uncertain outcomes; another Pod execution must not create another payment. A Job controller completion guarantee is not an exactly-once business-effect guarantee.

lessons.title: 20. Choose StatefulSet, DaemonSet or CronJob for the workload
lessons.takeaway: Deployments suit interchangeable Pods; StatefulSets give stable identity and storage, DaemonSets run one Pod per node, and CronJobs start Jobs on a schedule.

sections.title: Identity, placement and time
paragraphs: A Deployment (lesson 6) treats Pods as interchangeable: any replica can be replaced by a new one with a new name and empty scratch space. Some workloads need more. A StatefulSet gives each Pod a stable ordinal name (`queue-0`, `queue-1`), a stable DNS name through a headless Service, and its own PersistentVolumeClaim from `volumeClaimTemplates` that follows that name when the Pod is rescheduled. Pods start, update and stop in order by default. Use it for clustered databases, brokers and anything whose members must find each other by name.

A DaemonSet runs one Pod on every node, or every node that matches a selector, and adds one when a node joins. Node agents fit here: log shippers, metrics collectors, network and storage plugins. They often need host access, so review their privileges carefully (lesson 17).

A CronJob creates a Job (lesson 19) on a cron schedule. Set `timeZone` explicitly, `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` or `Replace` when overlapping runs would conflict, `startingDeadlineSeconds` so a missed schedule is skipped instead of run late, and history limits so finished Jobs are cleaned up. The Job itself must still be idempotent, because a run can be retried or, rarely, started twice.
sections.example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: queue
spec:
  clusterIP: None              # headless: DNS returns each Pod, not one virtual IP
  selector: {app: queue}
  ports: [{name: amqp, port: 5672}]
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: queue
spec:
  serviceName: queue           # Pods get stable names: queue-0.queue, queue-1.queue, ...
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: queue}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: queue}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: broker
        image: registry.example.test/queue:3.13.2
        ports: [{name: amqp, containerPort: 5672}]
        volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/queue}]
  volumeClaimTemplates:        # one PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod: data-queue-0, data-queue-1, ...
  - metadata: {name: data}
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      resources: {requests: {storage: 10Gi}}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: log-agent
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: log-agent}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: log-agent}
    spec:
      tolerations: [{operator: Exists}]       # also run on tainted nodes
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: registry.example.test/log-agent:1.4.2
        volumeMounts: [{name: logs, mountPath: /var/log, readOnly: true}]
      volumes: [{name: logs, hostPath: {path: /var/log}}]
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: nightly-report
spec:
  schedule: "30 2 * * *"       # 02:30 every day
  timeZone: Europe/London
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid    # skip a run while the previous one is still going
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 600
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 2
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
          - name: report
            image: registry.example.test/report:2.0.1
            args: ["--date", "yesterday"]

sections.title: What a StatefulSet does not do
paragraphs: A StatefulSet keeps names and volumes stable; it does not replicate data, elect leaders or back anything up. The application inside must handle clustering, and deleting or scaling down a StatefulSet does not delete its claims by default, so storage and its cost remain until you remove them on purpose (lesson 18). Managed database services are often a better choice than running stateful systems yourself.
These manifests were checked offline for consistent selectors, the headless Service name, volume names and a five-field schedule. They were not applied to a cluster.

exercise.prompt: For each workload, choose Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job or CronJob and give the deciding property: a stateless web API, a three-member etcd cluster, a node-level metrics exporter, a one-off database migration, a weekly cleanup of expired sessions.
exercise.solution: Web API: Deployment, because replicas are interchangeable. etcd cluster: StatefulSet, because members need stable names and their own persistent volumes. Metrics exporter: DaemonSet, because one Pod must run on every node. Database migration: Job, because it runs once to completion with bounded retries. Weekly cleanup: CronJob with concurrencyPolicy Forbid, an explicit time zone and an idempotent cleanup.
checks: Matches interchangeable replicas to a Deployment.
Uses a StatefulSet for stable identity and storage.
Uses a DaemonSet for per-node agents and Job/CronJob for finite and scheduled work.

lessons.title: 21. Scale from useful metrics and retain overload controls
lessons.takeaway: HorizontalPodAutoscaler changes replica count based on configured metrics.

sections.title: Scaling metrics and bounds
paragraphs: HorizontalPodAutoscaler changes replica count based on configured metrics. The optional autoscaling/v2 object targets 60% CPU utilization with bounds 2–4 and a scale-down stabilization window. CPU utilization depends on declared requests and the metrics API. A default local cluster may lack Metrics Server; applying the HPA can leave it unable to compute a recommendation.

sections.title: Readiness and downstream capacity
paragraphs: This calculation is simplified; readiness, missing metrics, tolerance and controller behavior matter. More replicas cannot repair a serialized database bottleneck or create shared scratch data. Maintain queue/admission controls and measure actual latency/error improvements before trusting autoscaling as an availability mechanism.
sections.example:
request 100m; observed 60m → 60% utilization
2 Pods averaging 90% at 60% target → rough desired ceil(2 × 90 / 60)=3
Bounds and stabilization then influence changes.

exercise.prompt: Why might kubectl get hpa show unknown metrics? Optional live cluster track: practice/optional-enforcement-track.md; document prerequisites and actual positive/negative results.
exercise.solution: Check the resource metrics API/Metrics Server, per-container requests and readiness rather than generating more arbitrary load. Install a reviewed compatible metrics add-on only in the opted-in local cluster, then record actual scaling and bounds.
checks: Verify metrics prerequisite.
Keep maximum replicas bounded.

options: CPU requests and an available resource metrics API
quiz.explanation: A CPU percentage target needs container CPU requests as its baseline and an available resource metrics API for observations. Accepted HPA configuration alone does not demonstrate actual scaling.

lessons.title: 22. Plan voluntary disruption without claiming universal availability
lessons.takeaway: PodDisruptionBudget limits certain voluntary evictions based on healthy availability.

sections.title: Voluntary eviction budgets
paragraphs: PodDisruptionBudget limits certain voluntary evictions based on healthy availability. With two replicas and `minAvailable` 1, an eviction request should retain at least one healthy instance when the mechanism applies. It does not prevent node crashes, application failures or all update actions. The optional `policy/v1` manifest selects the same app labels as the Deployment.

sections.title: Rollout and failure-domain limits
paragraphs: Rolling Deployment updates use their own rollout availability settings; a PDB is not a substitute for them. A single-node local cluster cannot demonstrate multi-zone resilience. Do not drain nodes in an existing shared cluster for this exercise; use paper timelines or a separately approved disposable local drill.
sections.example:
2 healthy Pods; minAvailable 1 → one voluntary eviction may proceed
1 healthy Pod → another eviction may beblocked
Unexpected node loss can violate desired availability anyway.

exercise.prompt: Could a PDB alone make a two-replica service survive a single-node outage?
exercise.solution: No if both replicas are on that node. Placement, node/failure-domain diversity, capacity and application data dependencies also determine availability. A PDB controls a specific voluntary-disruption boundary, not physical failures.
checks: Distinguish voluntary from involuntary failure.
Consider placement and capacity.

quiz.question: What does a PDB primarily constrain?
quiz.explanation: A PodDisruptionBudget constrains eligible voluntary evictions. It does not prevent node failure or guarantee availability when replicas share a failure domain.

lessons.title: 23. Render Helm configuration before enabling installation
lessons.takeaway: Helm packages parameterized manifests as charts.

sections.title: Chart values and rendering
paragraphs: Helm packages parameterized manifests as charts. Values customize templates, releases record installations and upgrades, and rendering exposes the resulting API objects. A chart does not make invalid selectors or unsafe privileges correct. The course uses a render-first exercise rather than shipping a flattened chart that would lose its expected directory structure in the downloadable bundle.

sections.title: Review before local installation
paragraphs: Pin a compatible Helm version, review actual generated defaults and compare the rendered workload with the known lab contract. No `helm install` command is required for offline study. If enabling the chart in the local cluster, preserve explicit context/namespace gates and local image settings; a default chart may select a different public image.

# Review generated Service, Deployment, values and remove unneeded defaults.
helm lint ./lab-chart
helm template release-demo ./lab-chart --namespace notebook-lab > rendered.yaml

exercise.solution: Inspect rendered selectors, Pod labels, Service target ports and probes together; linting alone does not test runtime routing. Treat rendered diffs as review artifacts and run server admission only after local context verification.

quiz.explanation: helm template. Inspect rendered selectors, Pod labels, Service target ports and probes together; linting alone does not test runtime routing. Treat rendered diffs as review artifacts and run server admission only after local context verification.

lessons.title: 24. Reconcile reviewed Git state and control drift
lessons.takeaway: GitOps controllers reconcile versioned desired state rather than treating a successful shell command as permanent truth.

sections.title: Desired-state reconciliation
paragraphs: GitOps controllers reconcile versioned desired state rather than treating a successful shell command as permanent truth. Separate application build from environment promotion, use immutable image identity and review desired-state changes. Manual changes can be overwritten on reconciliation. The lesson uses a timeline and rendered manifests; it does not install Flux, Argo CD or new CRDs into the local cluster.

sections.title: Controller permissions and pruning
paragraphs: A controller needs scoped API permissions and secret access appropriate to its work. Pruning can remove resources omitted from desired state, including data-bearing objects if carelessly managed. Bootstrap credentials, approvals and controller provenance are separate operational boundaries.
sections.example:
Git desired image v1 → controller applies v1
Manual kubectl sets image v2 → drift
Next reconcile may restore v1
Reviewed Gitpromotion changes desired state to v2

exercise.prompt: A rollback via kubectl succeeds but later v2 returns. Explain why.
exercise.solution: The repository still declares v2 and the controller reconciles it. Perform a reviewed Git revert/promotion back to the compatible v1 desired state, monitor reconciliation and account for schema/data changes separately.
checks: Explain source of truth and drift.
Review pruning/data consequences.

quiz.question: What should a durable GitOps rollback change?
options: The reviewed desired state in its source of truth
The database password in a public commit
quiz.explanation: A durable rollback changes the reviewed desired state in the controller's source of truth. An imperative change can be overwritten by reconciliation; data and schema compatibility require separate recovery evidence.
