lessons.title: 25. Set namespace guard rails and extend the API with custom resources
lessons.takeaway: ResourceQuota caps a namespace's total use and LimitRange sets per-container defaults; custom resources plus a controller let you manage new kinds of things the Kubernetes way.

sections.title: Quotas and limit ranges
paragraphs: When several teams share a cluster, one namespace can starve the others. A ResourceQuota caps the namespace's totals: requested CPU and memory, limits, number of Pods, claims or Services. Once a quota covers CPU or memory, every new Pod in the namespace must declare those requests, or admission rejects it.

A LimitRange sets defaults and bounds per container or Pod. It fills in a default request and limit when a manifest omits them, which lets quota-covered namespaces accept simple manifests, and it rejects containers asking for more than the maximum. Requests and limits themselves were covered in lesson 11.

Quotas are checked at admission, when objects are created; they do not stop a running process from using memory up to its limit. Combine them with RBAC (lesson 16) so teams cannot edit their own quotas.
sections.example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-budget
  namespace: notebook-lab
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "4"
    requests.memory: 8Gi
    limits.memory: 12Gi
    pods: "30"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "5"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: container-defaults
  namespace: notebook-lab
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    defaultRequest: {cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi}   # applied when a container sets no request
    default: {memory: 256Mi}                     # applied when a container sets no limit
    max: {memory: 2Gi}
---
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: backupschedules.ops.example.test
spec:
  group: ops.example.test
  scope: Namespaced
  names: {plural: backupschedules, singular: backupschedule, kind: BackupSchedule}
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          spec:
            type: object
            required: [database, schedule]
            properties:
              database: {type: string}
              schedule: {type: string}
              keepDays: {type: integer, minimum: 1, maximum: 90}
---
apiVersion: ops.example.test/v1
kind: BackupSchedule
metadata:
  name: orders-nightly
  namespace: notebook-lab
spec:
  database: orders
  schedule: "0 1 * * *"
  keepDays: 14

sections.title: Custom resources and operators
paragraphs: A CustomResourceDefinition adds a new kind to the API: once applied, `kubectl get backupschedules` works, objects are validated against the OpenAPI schema, and RBAC applies as for built-in kinds. A custom resource is only data. Something has to act on it.

An operator is a controller that watches custom resources and reconciles the real world toward them, exactly as the Deployment controller does for Pods (lesson 1). A database operator can create StatefulSets, run backups and perform failover from a short custom resource. Operators concentrate operational knowledge, but they run with broad permissions, and a buggy one can act on every resource it watches, so review their RBAC and upgrade them carefully.
The manifests were checked offline: the CRD's name matches its plural and group, and the BackupSchedule matches the CRD's group, version, kind and required fields. They were not applied to a cluster.

exercise.prompt: A namespace has a ResourceQuota on requests.cpu and requests.memory. A developer's Deployment with no resources section creates no Pods, and its ReplicaSet reports 'failed quota: must specify requests.cpu'. Explain the cause and two ways to fix it, saying which is better for the team.
exercise.solution: Once a quota covers CPU and memory requests, admission rejects Pods that do not declare them, so the ReplicaSet cannot create any. Fix 1: add resources.requests (and limits) to the Deployment, which is the better long-term practice because the values reflect the workload. Fix 2: add a LimitRange with defaultRequest and default values so omitted requests are filled in automatically, which is a good safety net for the namespace. Use both: the LimitRange prevents surprise failures, and explicit requests keep scheduling accurate.
checks: Explains that quota-covered resources must be declared.
Offers explicit requests and a LimitRange default.
Notes the ReplicaSet events as the evidence.

quiz.question: What happens when you apply a CustomResourceDefinition and create a custom resource, but no operator is installed?
options: Kubernetes runs the resource with default behaviour
The resource is stored and validated, but nothing acts on it
The API server refuses to store it
quiz.explanation: A CRD only extends the API. Behaviour comes from a controller that watches and reconciles the custom resources.

lessons.title: 26. Diagnose status, events, logs and network boundaries
lessons.takeaway: Troubleshooting follows the failed boundary: API rejection, Pending scheduling, container startup, readiness, Service routing, policy or application/data behavior.

sections.title: Failure stages and evidence
paragraphs: Troubleshooting follows the failed boundary: API rejection, Pending scheduling, container startup, readiness, Service routing, policy or application/data behavior. Inspect current conditions and recent events, then logs including a previous crashed container when available. Debug tooling should use the least privilege needed and avoid printing Secret contents. A fresh log line is evidence only for the process that emitted it.

sections.title: Missing images and debug privilege
paragraphs: `ImagePullBackOff`, `CrashLoopBackOff` and `Pending` indicate different stages, not interchangeable root causes. The kit's `imagePullPolicy` of `Never` intentionally fails if the named local image was not loaded onto kind nodes. A debug container or exec session is a separate privileged effect; use only the dedicated local lab.
sections.example:
kubectl --context=kind-notebook-lab -n notebook-lab describe pod NAME
kubectl --context=kind-notebook-lab -n notebook-lab logs NAME --previous
kubectl --context=kind-notebook-lab -n notebook-lab get endpointslices
# Use actual object names and check their readiness conditions.

sections.title: The order of checks changes the diagnosis
paragraphs: A user sees a connection failure. First inspect the Deployment and Pods: no scheduled Pod makes application HTTP logs irrelevant. If the Pod is Running, inspect Ready and EndpointSlices. If the endpoint is absent or unready, investigate selectors and probes before DNS. If a ready endpoint exists, compare a request to the Pod with a request through the Service; this separates application behavior from routing.

In the supplied workload `imagePullPolicy=Never` requires the image on each node that can host the Pod. `ErrImageNeverPull` can therefore affect one replica after rescheduling even if its sibling works. Increasing probe delays cannot load an image. Likewise, a readiness 503 cannot be corrected by repeatedly deleting Pods when every replacement receives the same broken configuration.
sections.example:
Pending -> scheduling conditions/events
ErrImageNeverPull -> local image on selected node
Running + Ready=False -> probe/app readiness
Ready=True + no matching endpoints -> Service selector
Ready endpoint + failed request -> traffic/app boundary

exercise.prompt: A replacement Pod reports ErrImageNeverPull; another replica serves traffic normally. Explain why a successful request to the healthy replica does not close the incident.
checks: Identify node-local image availability as the failed boundary under imagePullPolicy=Never.
Require recovery of the replacement replica and desired ready count; do not treat one successful response as deployment health.
exercise.solution: Inspect the failing Pod's assigned node and events, load the intended lab image through the documented kind procedure, then observe the replacement becoming Ready and rollout convergence. The healthy sibling proves only that one execution path works. Probe tuning or Service changes do not resolve the absent image.

quiz.question: A running Pod can still have no Service traffic because?
options: Readiness may fail even though its process runs
Running status also means Ready=True for every container
The Service uses the Deployment name rather than Pod labels to choose endpoints
quiz.explanation: A running process can fail its readiness probe, leaving its Pod ineligible for normal Service traffic. Inspect readiness and endpoints as well as process state; Running alone does not establish routability.

lessons.title: 27. Separate cluster backup, application restore and production readiness
lessons.takeaway: Cluster state backup preserves API objects and related control-plane state, while application data may live in volumes or external databases.

sections.title: Cluster state versus application data
paragraphs: Cluster state backup preserves API objects and related control-plane state, while application data may live in volumes or external databases. Recovering etcd does not restore every database byte or validate user invariants. Production planning includes multiple failure domains, access/identity controls, workload limits, reliable storage, observability, upgrades and tested recovery. A local kind exercise demonstrates only selected mechanics.

sections.title: Independent recovery verification
paragraphs: The lab PVC is not an off-node backup, and deleting the local cluster can remove its only copy. Use the delivery path SQLite restore test to understand independent data verification, then design provider-specific volume/database recovery. Never run etcd recovery commands against a shared cluster as a classroom shortcut.

Recovery inventory: Git desired manifests + protected Secrets +etcd state
Application: database backups/logs +volume snapshots if supported
Restore drill: rebuild platform → restore app data → verify business records → controlled traffic

exercise.solution: Identify each authoritative store, its supported backup method, protected/off-cluster copies and compatible restoration sequence. Verify known notes through the restored application, measure time/loss and list untested failure domains. Review platform upgrades against version skew and API deprecations.
checks: Separate control-plane and application data.
